Which ruler, who reigned jointly with his half-brother Ivan V until 1696, founded the Russian Navy and became Russia's first Emperor in 1721?
Peter the Great: Tsar of Russia from 1682 to 1725.

Marrying his first cousin, the reigning British queen, at age 20, this royal consort championed educational reform and the abolition of slavery, and organized the Great Exhibition of 1851 — who was he?
Prince Albert of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha
Prince Albert of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha: Consort of Queen Victoria from 1840 to 1861.
Prince Albert of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha
Third pharaoh of the Nineteenth Dynasty, he waged 15 military campaigns and reigned 66 years — the longest recorded of any pharaoh — earning the title 'the Great.' Who was he?
Ramesses II: Pharaoh of Egypt from 1279 to 1213 BC.
An Italian neurobiologist who shared the 1986 Nobel for discovering nerve growth factor and served as a senator for life, she became the first Nobel laureate to turn 100 — who is she?

Serving as Ukraine's Defence Minister from 2023 to 2025 before becoming Secretary of the National Security and Defence Council, this Crimean Tatar politician has co-chaired a Crimea diplomatic initiative since 2020 — who is he?
The youngest person ever to hold the office, this Filipino politician became her country's vice president after serving multiple terms as mayor of Davao City — who is she?
Sara Duterte: Vice President of the Philippines since 2022.
Born after his brother Abel was murdered by their brother Cain, this third son of Adam and Eve was believed by his mother to be sent by God as a replacement — who is he?
Seth: Third son of Adam and Eve. The Hebrew Bible names two of his siblings as Cain and Abel.
Also called 'the Canaanite,' this apostle of Jesus was omitted from Jerome's fourth-century collection of biographies despite some writings falsely attributed to him — who is he?
Simon the Zealot: Apostle of Jesus.

Before the Civil War he taught at the Virginia Military Institute; historians rank this Confederate general among the most gifted tacticians in U.S. history, and he died in 1863 from wounds in the war's eastern theater — who was he?
Stonewall Jackson: Confederate States Army general (1824–1863)
This Umayyad commander crossed from North Africa to launch the Muslim conquest of the Iberian Peninsula in 711, leaving his name forever attached to the rock where he massed his troops — who is he?
Tariq ibn Ziyad: Umayyad commander in Hispania (died c. 720)
Before becoming the Supreme Court's first African-American justice, he argued 32 civil rights cases before it and won 29 — culminating in the landmark Brown v. Board of Education. Who was he?
Thurgood Marshall: US Supreme Court justice from 1967 to 1991.

Political theorist Roger Griffin traced this extreme, supremacist strain of national pride — an ideological foundation beneath Fascist Italy and Nazi Germany — to the view of nations as living organisms with 'great cultural destinies.' What's it called?
A former central bank governor who tamed hyperinflation, he became Ukraine's third president in 2005 on a platform of turning the country toward the EU and NATO. Who is he?
Viktor Yushchenko: President of Ukraine from 2005 to 2010.
Best known for playing 'Trapper' John McIntyre on the CBS series M*A*S*H, this actor later became a regular panelist on a Fox News investing show — who is he?
Hieronymus Karl Friedrich, Freiherr von Münchhausen
Fought between 1939 and 1945, this global conflict remains history's deadliest, claiming 60 to 75 million lives and ending with the only nuclear weapons ever used in war — which conflict?
World War II: 1939–1945 global conflict. World War II, or the Second World War (1 September 1939 – 2 September 1945), was a global conflict between two coalitions: the Allies and the Axis powers.

Regarded as the fourth person to accept Islam, this former slave became the adopted son of the Prophet Muhammad and later commanded early Muslim military expeditions, including a final raid on Byzantine-held Bosra in 629 CE — who was he?
Zayd ibn Haritha al-Kalbi: Companion and adopted son of the Islamic prophet Muhammad.
Who among these four was born earliest?
Ellen Swallow Richards (born 1842) is the earliest of the four. Richards graduated from Westford Academy (second oldest secondary school in Massachusetts) in 1862.
Who among these four was born earliest?
Benjamin Banneker (born 1731) is the earliest of the four. Benjamin Banneker (November 9, 1731 – October 19, 1806) was an American naturalist, mathematician, astronomer and almanac author.
Which one below was born first?

Omar Khayyam (born 1048) is the earliest of the four. Omar Khayyam (1048–1131) was a Persian poet and polymath, known for his contributions to mathematics, astronomy, philosophy, and Persian literature.
Which one below was established earliest?
COBOL (founded 1959) is the earliest of the four. COBOL (Common Business-Oriented Language;) is a compiled English-like computer programming language designed for business use.
Which of these four was released earliest?
Pascal (programming language) (published 1972) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four is a physicist?
Edwin McMillan is a physicist. McMillan co-invented the synchrotron with Vladimir Veksler, and after the war he returned to the Berkeley Radiation Laboratory to build them.
Who among these is a chemist?
Henry Taube is a chemist. Taube completed his undergraduate and master's degrees at the University of Saskatchewan, and his PhD from the University of California, Berkeley.
What is the atomic number of Sodium?
Sodium is a chemical element; it has symbol Na (from Neo-Latin natrium) and atomic number 11.
In what year was Viktor Yushchenko born?
Viktor Yushchenko: Yushchenko's first career was in the banking industry.
In what year was Giordano Bruno born?
Giordano Bruno: Bruno's pantheism was not taken lightly by the church, nor was his teaching of metempsychosis regarding the reincarnation of the soul.
In what year was Tomitaro Makino born?
Tomitaro Makino (牧野 富太郎, Makino Tomitarō; 24 April 1862 – 18 January 1957) was a pioneer Japanese botanist noted for his taxonomic work.
In what year did Paul Allen die?
Paul Allen: Paul Gardner Allen (January 21, 1953 – October 15, 2018) was an American businessman, computer programmer, and investor.
In what year did Mikhail Lomonosov die?
Mikhail Lomonosov: One of the founders of modern geology, Lomonosov was also a poet and influenced the formation of the modern Russian literary language.
In what year was Scurvy discovered?
Scurvy or scorbutus is a deficiency disease (state of malnutrition) resulting from a lack of vitamin C (ascorbic acid).
In what year was Polonium discovered?
Polonium is a chemical element; it has symbol Po and atomic number 84.
Spironolactone: Pfizer. Spironolactone, sold under the brand name Aldactone among others, is classed as a diuretic medication.
In which country is Gaboon viper?
Gaboon viper: Gabon. It is the largest member of the genus Bitis.
Who is credited with discovering Radon?
Radon: Friedrich Ernst Dorn. Radon is a chemical element; it has symbol Rn and atomic number 86.
Who is credited with discovering Tautavel Man?
Tautavel Man: Henry de Lumley. Tautavel Man refers to the archaic humans which—from approximately 550,000 to 400,000 years ago—inhabited the Caune de l’Arago, a limestone cave in Tautavel, France.
Who is credited with discovering MDMA?
MDMA: Anton Köllisch. MDMA was first synthesized in 1912 by Merck chemist Anton Köllisch.
In this science fiction comedy-drama, a man undergoes a procedure to shrink his body and start a new life in a miniature experimental community. What film is it?
Adansonia is a genus of medium-to-large deciduous trees known as baobabs or boababs.

With roughly 370 million individuals, this migratory thrush outnumbers red-winged blackbirds and starlings across its home continent, despite being misnamed after an unrelated European species — what is it?
American robin (Turdus migratorius) is a migratory bird of the true thrush genus and Turdidae, the wider thrush family.
Largely self-taught, this Dutch tradesman-turned-scientist pioneered the use of the microscope and is commonly called the 'Father of Microbiology' — who is he?
Antonie van Leeuwenhoek (AHN-tə-nee vahn LAY-vən-hook, -huuk; 24 October 1632 - 26 August 1723) was a Dutch microbiologist and microscopist in the Golden Age of Dutch art, science and technology.
This British mathematician coined the term 'mathematical induction' and is best remembered for a pair of laws linking conjunction, disjunction, and negation in logic — who was he?
Augustus De Morgan (27 June 1806 - 18 March 1871) was a British mathematician and logician.
Usually the tenth-brightest star in the night sky, this red supergiant in the constellation Orion varies noticeably in brightness over a roughly 400-day cycle — name the star?
Betelgeuse is a red supergiant star in the equatorial constellation of Orion. Its Bayer designation is α Orionis, Latinised to Alpha Orionis and abbreviated Alpha Ori or α Ori.
First described in 1903 from fossils found in Colorado, this sauropod dinosaur's Greek name means arm lizard, a reference to its proportionately long front limbs — what genus is it?
Brachiosaurus is a genus of sauropod dinosaur that lived in North America during the Late Jurassic, about 155.6 to 145.5 million years ago.
The leaves and buds of this evergreen shrub, when processed differently, yield green, black, oolong, white, and yellow varieties of the world's most popular hot beverage — what's the species?
Camellia sinensis is a species of evergreen shrub or small tree in the flowering plant family Theaceae.
Taken by mouth with effects lasting about a day, this second-generation antihistamine treats hay fever, hives, and dermatitis with less drowsiness than older allergy medications — what is it?
Cetirizine is a second-generation peripherally selective antihistamine used to treat allergic rhinitis (hay fever), dermatitis, urticaria (hives), and runny nose.
Marked by a stopped heartbeat and halted breathing, this reversible-sounding medical state was given its name once CPR and defibrillation made post-arrest resuscitation possible — what's it called?
Clinical death is the medical term for cessation of blood circulation and breathing, the two criteria necessary to sustain the lives of human beings and of many other organisms.
Born in 1863, this Italian mathematician is remembered chiefly as a major contributor to the early development of algebraic geometry — who was he?
Corrado Segre (20 August 1863 - 18 May 1924) was an Italian mathematician who is remembered today as a major contributor to the early development of algebraic geometry.

Native to Madagascar and grown as an ornamental tree throughout the tropics, this legume species has fern-like leaves and a flamboyant summer display of orange-red flowers; its wild origin wasn't confirmed until 1932. What tree is this?
Delonix regia is a species of flowering plant in the bean family Fabaceae, subfamily Caesalpinioideae native to Madagascar.

This American entrepreneur co-founded Facebook alongside Mark Zuckerberg, then left in 2008 to co-found the productivity company Asana, becoming the youngest self-made billionaire in the world by 2011 — who is he?

Dustin Moskovitz (born May 22, 1984) is an American internet entrepreneur who co-founded the social media service Facebook and its parent company Meta Platforms with Mark Zuckerberg, Eduardo Saverin, Andrew McCollum and Chris Hughes.
Practitioners of this zoological discipline have identified more than 1.3 million species within a single group of arthropods — what is it called?
Entomology (ntomon), meaning "insect", and (lgos), meaning "study", is the branch of zoology that focuses on insects.
Immature at birth but developed by puberty, this network of organs includes the vagina, uterus, and fallopian tubes, protected by a fold called the labia majora — what's it called?
Female reproductive system is made up of the internal and external sex organs that function in the reproduction of new offspring.

A French economist who gave lectures up and down the country and helped found the Inter-Parliamentary Union, he shared the very first Nobel Peace Prize in 1901 for his work in Europe's peace movement — who was he?
Frédéric Passy (20 May 1822 - 12 June 1912) was a French economist and pacifist who was a founding member of several peace societies and the Inter-Parliamentary Union.
Caused in over 90% of cases by iodine deficiency, this visible swelling in the neck comes from an enlarged thyroid gland — name the condition?
Goitre (British English, spelled goiter in American English) is a swelling in the neck resulting from an enlarged thyroid gland.
About the size of a closed fist and tucked between the lungs, this four-chambered muscular organ pumps blood throughout the body — name it?
Heart is a muscular organ found in humans and other animals.
Native to Japan, this deciduous shrub grows big flower heads that can turn pink or blue and is also known as the mophead or lacecap — which plant?
Hydrangea macrophylla is a species of flowering plant in the family Hydrangeaceae, native and endemic to Japan.
These creatures don't breathe through a nose or lungs — air enters through tiny paired openings along their sides, piped straight to the tissues. What hexapod group are they?
Insect (from Latin insectum) are hexapod invertebrates of the class Insecta.
This German polymath wrote The Sorrows of Young Werther and essays on botany, anatomy, and color theory—he's the most influential writer in the German language. Who was he?
Johann Wolfgang von Goethe (28 August 1749 - 22 March 1832) was a German polymath who is widely regarded as the most influential writer in the German language.
About the size of a domestic chicken, these flightless New Zealand natives turn out to be more closely related to Madagascar's extinct elephant birds than to the giant moa — what are they?
Kiwi (bird) are flightless birds endemic to New Zealand of the order Apterygiformes.
This Chinese herbalist, martial artist, and tactical advisor died in 1933 claiming a birth year of 1677 — a longevity claim gerontologists now regard as myth — who was he?
Li Ching-Yuen (simplified; traditional; pinyin: L Qngyn, died 6 May 1933) was a Chinese herbalist, martial artist and tactical advisor, known for his supposed extreme longevity.
Caused by a compromised lymphatic system, this condition raises infection risk in affected tissue and is treated with compression and massage rather than water pills — what is it?
Lymphedema (USA), lymphoedema (UK) also known as lymphatic edema (US)/oedema (UK), is a condition of localized swelling caused by a compromised lymphatic system.
This genus of flowering plants belongs to the chamomile tribe of the sunflower family, and several of its species go by the folk name 'mayweed' — which genus?
Matricaria is a genus of flowering plants in the chamomile tribe within the sunflower family.
First flown by the Soviet Air Force in 1968 and still in Russian production today, this medium chopper carries the NATO reporting name 'Hip' — what aircraft is it?
Mil Mi-8 is a family of medium twin-turbine helicopters, originally designed by the Soviet Central Aerohydrodynamic Institute (TsAGI) in the 1960s and introduced into the Soviet Air Force in 1968.

Caused when fly larvae burrow into and feed on an animal's tissue, this parasitic infestation is triggered by open wounds but can occur on unbroken skin when species such as the botfly are involved — name this condition?
Myiasis (my-), also known as flystrike or fly strike, is the parasitic infestation of the body of a live animal by fly larvae (maggots) that grow inside the host while feeding on its tissue.

Jointly operated by the U.S. Air Force and NASA in the 1960s, this rocket-powered experimental aircraft set speed and altitude records, once reaching Mach 6.7 and crossing into the edge of outer space — name this aircraft?

North American X-15 is a hypersonic rocket-powered aircraft formerly operated by the United States Air Force and the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) as part of the X-plane series of experimental aircraft.
Triggered by a surge of luteinizing hormone near the midpoint of the cycle, this event sees an ovarian follicle rupture and release an egg ready to be fertilized. What's the term?
Ovulation is an important part of the menstrual cycle in female vertebrates where the egg cells are released from the ovaries as part of the ovarian cycle.

This short-acting barbiturate is used as a sedative and anticonvulsant in low doses, but in high doses causes fatal respiratory arrest, making it a drug of choice for both veterinary euthanasia and U.S. executions — what is it?
Pentobarbital (US) or pentobarbitone (British and Australian) is a short-acting barbiturate typically used as a sedative, a preanesthetic, and to control convulsions in emergencies.
Equal to one-eighth of a gallon in both the imperial and US customary systems, this unit of volume is just over 20% larger in Britain than it is in America — name it?
Pint (symbol pt, sometimes abbreviated as p) is a unit of volume or capacity in both the imperial and United States customary measurement systems.

This corticosteroid drug treats a huge range of conditions — from rheumatoid arthritis and asthma to eye inflammation and certain cancers — and can be taken orally, injected, or applied to the skin. What is it?
Prednisolone is a corticosteroid, a steroid hormone used to treat certain types of allergies, inflammatory conditions, autoimmune disorders, and cancers, electrolyte imbalances, and skin conditions.
A zoonotic virus that triggers violent movements, a dread of water, and almost certain death once symptoms set in — usually one to three months after exposure. What is this disease?
Rabies is a zoonotic viral disease that causes acute and severe encephalitis in humans and other mammals.
Made by steaming dehusked oat groats before flattening them under heavy rollers and lightly toasting them, this whole-grain food becomes porridge when cooked — which product?
Rolled oats are a type of lightly processed whole-grain food.
Before becoming a full-time cartoonist in 1995, this creator of a hit workplace-satire comic strip worked various corporate jobs — who is he?
Scott Adams (June 8, 1957 - January 13, 2026) was an American cartoonist, author, and commentator.
Typically a bony enclosure around a vertebrate's brain, though cartilage in some fish and amphibians, this head structure combines a neurocranium with a facial skeleton — name it?

Skull is typically a bony enclosure around the brain of a vertebrate. In a human, the skull comprises two prominent parts: the neurocranium and the facial skeleton, which evolved from the first pharyngeal arch.
Named from the Greek word for tallow, this soft waxy 18-carbon saturated fatty compound is common in animal fats like beef tallow and lard — what is it called?
Stearic acid (stee-) is a saturated fatty acid with an 18-carbon chain.

Named after a figure from Greek mythology condemned to eternal frustration, this hard, corrosion-resistant blue-gray metal, atomic number 73, is mined alongside the chemically similar niobium in the ore known as coltan. What element is this?
Tantalum is a chemical element; it has symbol Ta and atomic number 73.
The largest member of the genus Panthera and an apex predator of Asian forests, this big cat wears orange fur striped in mostly-vertical black — what is it?
Tiger (Panthera tigris) is a large cat and a member of the genus Panthera native to Asia.
This broad category of large, hoofed mammals was reclassified in 2001 into a new clade after genetic data revealed the older grouping wasn't a true evolutionary lineage. Name the category of animals?
Ungulate are members of the diverse clade Euungulata, which primarily consists of large mammals with hooves.
This unit of time, equal to seven days, serves as the standard calendrical period between a day and a month in most of the world. What is it?
Week (in the Western and international context) is a unit of time equal to seven days.
First synthesized by chemist Alexander Shulgin in 1974, this psychedelic compound produces hallucinogenic effects considered milder than LSD or psilocybin — what is it commonly known as?
2C-B: Psychedelic drug. 2C-B, also known as 4-bromo-2,5-dimethoxyphenethylamine or by names such as Nexus or Erox, is a psychedelic drug of the phenethylamine and 2C families.
Also known as the buckeye or conker tree, this deciduous flowering tree is often confused with the unrelated sweet chestnut — which species?
Aesculus hippocastanum: Species of tree in the soapberry family.
Named for its carbon-carbon double bond, this class of hydrocarbon includes terminal versions known as alpha-olefins — what's the general term for it?
Alkene: Hydrocarbon compound containing one or more C=C bonds.
This group of diseases occurs when misfolded proteins accumulate in body tissue, causing fatigue, swelling, and shortness of breath among roughly 36 distinct protein-driven types — what is it?
Amyloidosis: Metabolic disease involving abnormal deposited amyloid proteins.
Unlike fear, which responds to a threat that's already here, this emotional state involves dread over something that hasn't happened yet, often paired with pacing and rumination. What is it?
Native to Eurasia, this perennial plant is grown as a vegetable crop for its tender young shoots, harvested in the spring — what's this vegetable?
Asparagus: Species of flowering plant in the family Asparagaceae.
A Kenyan economist who met his future wife at the University of Hawaii, this man became the father of a future U.S. president and the subject of that son's 1995 memoir — who is he?
Both heads of this upper-arm muscle originate on the scapula and let you flex your elbow while turning your palm upward — what muscle is it?

Biceps: Muscle on the front of the upper arm. While the long head of the biceps crosses both the shoulder and elbow joints, its main function is at the elbow where it flexes and supinates the forearm.
Named in allusion to a 'Flying Fortress' that came before it, this pressurized WWII heavy bomber dropped the atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki. Which aircraft?
Air warfare of World War II
Boeing B-29 Superfortress: US heavy bomber aircraft, 1942.
Nicknamed 'angel's trumpets' for its pendulous, fragrant blooms, this toxic nightshade-family genus is officially Extinct in the Wild yet thrives worldwide as a garden plant — which genus?
Brugmansia: Genus of flowering plants in the nightshade family.
Present in the gut or mouth of up to 60 percent of healthy adults, this opportunistic yeast turns dangerous in immunocompromised patients, causing a common fungal infection — what species is it?
Candida albicans: Species of fungus. Candida albicans is an opportunistic pathogenic yeast that is a common member of the human gut flora.
Named after a Louisiana parish and named the state's official canine in 1979, this herding breed was traditionally used to hunt feral boars — what breed is it?
Catahoula Leopard Dog: American breed of dog.
Known as lamb's quarters, goosefoot, or fat-hen, this fast-growing annual weed in the amaranth family is sometimes cultivated as food elsewhere — which plant?
Chenopodium album: Species of flowering plant in the goosefoot family.
This lincosamide antibiotic treats infections from strep throat to acne, but raises the risk of a specific gut infection roughly fourfold — what is it?
Clindamycin: Antibiotic. It can also be used to treat acne, and some cases of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA).
Best known for its powerful, beautiful song, this small Old World flycatcher sometimes hybridizes with a closely related thrush species where their ranges overlap — which bird?
Common nightingale: Species of bird. Its range partly overlaps with that of the more northerly thrush nightingale (Luscinia luscinia), a closely related species with which hybrids have occurred.
Also known as hawthorn, quickthorn, or May-tree, this genus of several hundred shrub and tree species in the rose family is native across the temperate Northern Hemisphere — which genus?
Crataegus: Genus of flowering plants in the rose family Rosaceae.

Developed as a successor to an earlier delta-wing fighter family, this French all-weather interceptor entered service with the French Air Force in 1974, equipped with Cyrano IV radar — what aircraft is it?
Dassault Mirage F1: French attack aircraft. During the 1960s, Dassault commenced development of what would become the Mirage F1 as a private venture, alongside the larger Mirage F2.
Native to North Africa and West Asia, this annual herb in the celery family lends its leaves and seeds as both an herb and a spice — what is it?
Dill: Species of flowering plant in the celery family Apiaceae.

This medical term covers abnormal cell or organ growth — from hip conditions to bone marrow disorders — and is generally distinguished from cancerous neoplasia, though some forms are precancerous. What is it called?
Dysplasia: Abnormal development, at macroscopic or microscopical level.

In this lung disease the walls between the alveoli break down, merging tiny air sacs into enlarged spaces that shrink the surface available for gas exchange and starve the blood of oxygen. Which condition is it?
Emphysema: Chronic lung condition. Emphysema is a condition of the lung marked by abnormal enlargement of the alveoli with loss of pulmonary elasticity.
This Hungarian-American theoretical physicist won the 1963 Nobel for applying fundamental symmetry principles to the atomic nucleus and elementary particles — who was he?
Eugene Wigner: Hungarian-American physicist and mathematician (1902–1995)
Found on birds and even some non-avian dinosaurs, this complex evolutionary structure aids flight, insulation and waterproofing, and gives its name to the study of plumology — what is it?

Members of this insect order have just one pair of true wings — the hindwings evolved into balance organs called halteres — and the group includes mosquitoes among its 150,000+ species. What are they commonly called?
Fly: Order of insects. A fly (pl. flies) is an insect of the order Diptera (from Ancient Greek δι- di- 'two' and πτερόν pteron 'wing'), named for the single pair of wings.
Capable of living up to 177 years and weighing as much as 417 kilograms, which giant reptile — native to a chain of Pacific islands named for it — is the largest cold-blooded land animal alive today?
Galápagos tortoise: Species of reptile. The species comprises 15 subspecies (12 extant and 3 extinct).
The tallest land animal alive and the largest ruminant on Earth, its closest living relative is the okapi — which long-necked African mammal is it?

This algebraic structure — a set paired with an operation that's associative, has an identity element, and gives every member an inverse — is exemplified by the integers under addition. What is it called?

Group (mathematics): Set with associative invertible operation. The concept of a group was elaborated for handling, in a unified way, many mathematical structures such as numbers, geometric shapes and polynomial roots.
About the size of a closed fist and enclosed in a protective sac called the pericardium, this four-chambered organ sits in the chest between the lungs and pumps blood through the body — which organ?
Heart: Organ found in humans and other animals.
Named for the English physician who first described it in 1832, this cancer is defined by multinucleated Reed–Sternberg cells in the lymph nodes — what is it?
Hodgkin lymphoma: Type of blood and immune-system cancer.
Named from Greek words meaning "over" and "formation," this condition enlarges tissue by increasing the number of cells rather than their size — which term, distinct from hypertrophy?
Hyperplasia: Enlargement of tissue due to cell proliferation.
Commonly known as chaga, this parasitic fungus grows on birch trees and forms a charcoal-like black mass often marketed, questionably, as a health supplement — what's its scientific name?
Inonotus obliquus: Species of fungus. Inonotus obliquus, commonly called chaga (a Latinization of the Russian word ча́га), is a fungus in the family Hymenochaetaceae.
The first woman to chair the Federal Reserve, this American economist later became the first woman to serve as U.S. Treasury secretary — who is she?
Janet Yellen: American economist and government official (born 1946)
Named the type genus of the walnut family, this group of deciduous trees produces the walnuts eaten worldwide, with China responsible for half the global supply — which genus?
Juglans: Genus of trees. Walnut trees are any species of tree in the plant genus Juglans, the type genus of the family Juglandaceae, the seeds of which are referred to as walnuts.
Caused by a thiamine deficiency often linked to heavy alcohol use, this brain disorder is marked by amnesia and confabulation, and frequently pairs with Wernicke encephalopathy — which condition?
Korsakoff syndrome: Mental illness caused by a lack of thiamine in the brain.
Distinguished by coloured scales, large triangular wings, and a nectar-sipping proboscis, which insect order encompasses both butterflies and moths?
Lepidoptera: Order of insects including moths and butterflies.
Based on the L-188 Electra airliner and distinguished by a tail 'stinger' used to magnetically detect submarines, this four-engine turboprop has served the US Navy since the 1960s — which aircraft?
Lockheed P-3 Orion: Maritime patrol and anti-submarine aircraft family.
Known historically as 'magnesia alba' to distinguish it from a manganese-containing mineral called 'magnesia nigra,' this white hygroscopic solid has the formula MgO — what is it?
Magnesium oxide: Chemical compound naturally occurring as periclase.
Among the first women in Canada to earn a medical doctorate, this physician-chemist is best known for her 1913 work with Leonor Michaelis on enzyme kinetics — who was she?
Maud Menten: Canadian physician and chemist (1879–1960)
Marketed under brand names like Quaalude and Sopor, this sedative was pulled from commercial production in the mid-1980s due to widespread misuse — which drug?
This synthetic prostaglandin medication treats stomach ulcers, induces labor, and — often paired with mifepristone — is used to end a pregnancy. What drug is it?
Misoprostol: Medication to induce abortion and treat ulcers.

Grouping over 30 inherited disorders that cause progressive weakening and wasting of skeletal tissue — with the Duchenne form affecting roughly half of all cases in young boys — what's this disease group called?
Muscular dystrophy: Diseases in which skeletal and visceral muscles break down over time.

First arising in wormlike organisms 550 to 600 million years ago, this body-wide network splits into a central hub of brain and spinal cord and a peripheral web of nerve fibers relaying signals to and from every body part — which network?
Nervous system: Part of an animal that coordinates actions and senses.
Practitioners of this field are sometimes mistaken for mere coin collectors, but they study all means of paying debts — even the horses the Kyrgyz once used as currency. What's the field called?
Numismatics: Study of currencies, coins and paper money.
Described as far back as the 300s BC by Hippocrates, this bone infection most often strikes the spine in adults and the long bones in children — which condition?
Osteomyelitis: Infection of the bones. It may be acute or chronic and can be classified as hematogenous or non-hematogenous.

Native to southern Brazil, Paraguay and northern Argentina, this vine produces a round berry that turns yellow or dark purple at maturity, prized for its juicy, seed-filled interior — what is it, scientifically speaking?
Passiflora edulis: Species of flowering plant in the passion flower family.
Known online by the alias 'brokep,' this Swedish-born entrepreneur co-founded a famous BitTorrent search engine before launching the privacy-focused registrar Njalla in 2017 — who is he?
Peter Sunde: Swedish entrepreneur and politician. Peter Sunde Kolmisoppi (born 13 September 1978), alias brokep, is a Swedish-born Finnish-Norwegian entrepreneur and politician.
Known as the Scots pine in Britain, this Eurasian conifer is identifiable by its blue-green needles and orange-red bark — which species?
Pinus sylvestris: Species of conifer. Pinus sylvestris is a species of tree in the pine family Pinaceae that is native to Eurasia.
Also known as niter or saltpeter, this compound is a key ingredient of traditional gunpowder and gives cured meats their reddish color — what is it?
Potassium nitrate: Chemical compound. Potassium nitrate is a chemical compound with a sharp, salty, bitter taste and the chemical formula KNO3.
Fossils of this genus, found in Germany's Solnhofen limestone, mark the first pterosaur ever identified as a flying reptile — which genus?
Pterodactylus: Genus of pterodactyloid pterosaur from the Late Jurassic.
This genus of muroid rodents gives its scientific name to the common rat, though not every animal called a rat actually belongs to it — which genus?
Sold under the brand name Rituxan, this monoclonal antibody treats non-Hodgkin lymphoma, rheumatoid arthritis and several other autoimmune conditions via slow IV infusion — what is it?
